summary:
Extremadura stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado as BOE-A-2023-5366, which establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. The law mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields, with public authorities acting within their competences; its education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by the autonomous communities, and the Extremadura regional government is among the governments that carry them out.

Title II of the law regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route with no medical diagnosis and no requirement of two years of medical treatment, and with corresponding adaptation of identity documents. The former age-majority requirement for requesting rectification has been removed, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules in Extremadura as elsewhere in Spain.

Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Extremadura records the lowest per-capita rate of hate offences of any Spanish autonomous community in national statistics. That figure reflects how little is counted rather than demonstrated protection, and the low count should not be read as reassurance: a visitor's exposure otherwise tracks the national framework and its enforcement.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied in Spain since 2005.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch assessed the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition, and reported its passage by the Spanish Congress of Deputies on 16 February 2023 as legal gender recognition by self-identification through a simple administrative process.

With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay, and is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.

The age-12 recognition provision provoked political conflict at national level, and the regional government's posture toward implementation in Extremadura is not addressed by any source in this inventory.

The hate-crime aggravation and the hate-speech offence rest on Organic Law 6/2022 rather than on Ley 4/2023, so the visitor-facing protection machinery depends on two separate statutes. The two enforcement cases on file, in Vigo and in Valencia, are drawn from other autonomous communities and show how the aggravation has been applied, not an Extremadura prosecution.
localsOnly:
Ley 4/2023 mandates measures in workplace and health fields as well as in education, all delivered by public authorities acting within their competences, with the autonomous community responsible for the education-facing and administrative provisions. Human Rights Watch reports that the law strengthens sexuality education.

The law bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before their consent, and enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples.

Prohibitions on LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing apply to residents in their ordinary service relationships, and children from age 12 may obtain legal recognition under certain conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict.

Consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16 is regulated by the national law rather than left to clinical discretion alone.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory documents an Extremadura-specific implementing decree, regional decree or circular setting out how the regional government applies the administrative and education-facing provisions of Ley 4/2023. The extent of regional implementing measures therefore remains unresolved here.

No source describes a visitor in Extremadura being refused entry to a sex-separated facility, questioned on their documents, or screened at a border or checkpoint on the basis of a gender marker. The facility rule is stated in the legal framework; its practical application to visitors is not sourced.

The claim that Extremadura records the lowest per-capita hate-offence rate is carried without the underlying dataset, the counting period or a breakdown by offence type in this inventory. Whether the low figure reflects underreporting to police or under-classification by prosecutors is asserted rather than demonstrated by a source here.

No Extremadura-specific hate-crime prosecution, sentencing or police report concerning a trans victim is sourced; the two cases on file are from Vigo and Valencia. Regional civil-registry practice on document adaptation, and any waiting times or refusals at registries in Extremadura, are likewise not sourced.
